In the July report on Mauritania, the UN Special Rapporteur on contemporary forms of slavery noted the persistence of both descent-based and modern forms of slavery in certain parts of the country, and highlighted the social, economic and political exclusion experienced by currently and formerly enslaved individuals and their descendants.

The Tekavoul social transfer program covers 133,510 extremely poor households, with 56,581 financed by the project and 76,929 by the government budget. The social register includes over 200,000 households, representing a third of the Mauritanian population, and covers the entire country.

The Mauritanian government has decided to scale up the Tekavoul programme nationwide, increasing the amount of the quarterly cash transfer per household from 1,500 to 2,200 in 2021, then 2,900 in 2023 and reaching 3,600 MRU in 2024. The World Bank is supporting the deployment of the national Social Registry, the TEKAVOUL social transfer program, and its shock-responsive social safety net program, ELMAOUNA.
